intent: How many articles are there on Morocco that were published in 2009?

annotation.notes: Count question, gold spelled out ('One'); number_match parses both 'one' and '1'. The gold is a bare 'One', so the spec cannot additionally require the word 'article' (that would reject the gold itself). Medium confidence: 1 is a low-discriminative value and an answer that states a wrong total while mentioning '1' somewhere (e.g. '3 articles, 1 of them from 2010') would slip through. Realistic wrong answers state a different count and are rejected. The year 2009 in the answer is harmless because 1 is still required.

intent: Were these two articles published on the same day: Bayern beating Dortmund 5-4 on penalties in the German Super Cup, and Dortmund signing Ousmane Dembele?

annotation.notes: Straight yes/no gold, standard recipe. first_sentence keeps a trailing justification ('...no other article that day') from tripping the must_exclude. Word-boundary matching means 'no' cannot fire inside 'not'/'nothing'.

intent: Follow this navigation path: Search Boston, visit the fifth result from the first page, identify the second state in the body/content of the article, and search the state. Visit the third link from the search result and tell me the name of the first state in the content/body of the final article. If you encounter a redirect link at any point, then visit that link. If any of the articles are not found, then report the task as incomplete.

annotation.notes: Single named entity; neither the gold nor a competing state is named in the intent, so plain must_include is safe from trap 1. Full scope because this is a long navigation chain and correct answers frequently open with narration of the path. Residual risk (hence medium): if the intermediate state on the path is also Colorado, a wrong answer that reports the chain would contain the token.

intent: Navigate to the 11th article when you search "murder case". Then take the first two words from the main content of the visited article and search them. Report the name of the last article in the search results.

reference_answers.fuzzy_match: Wikinews interviews former Salt Lake City mayor and 2012 presidential candidate Rocky Anderson

annotation.notes: Long Wikinews headline; requiring the whole title would reject correct answers that paraphrase or truncate it. 'Rocky Anderson' is the unique, load-bearing part of the title and appears nowhere in the intent. Deliberately not requiring 'Salt Lake City' too -- a correct answer may shorten the headline to the interviewee's name.

intent: Could you list all the news articles on the most recent diesel emission scandal at Volkswagen?

items: engulfed by diesel emissions scandal |OR| engulfed by diesel emission scandal
emissions scandal may affect thousands more cars |OR| emission scandal may affect thousands more cars |OR| may affect thousands more cars
ceo resigns after emissions scandal |OR| ceo resigns after emission scandal

reference_answers.fuzzy_match: Volkswagen engulfed by diesel emissions scandal, Volkswagen emissions scandal may affect thousands more cars, Volkswagen CEO resigns after emissions scandal

annotation.notes: Three article titles must all be listed. Each item keeps the distinctive tail of its title rather than the full string, so a 'VW' abbreviation or a dropped leading 'Volkswagen' still matches, while the fragments remain unique enough that no single article can satisfy two items. No order is requested, so ordered stays false.

intent: List the names of all the animals mentioned in these articles: "England: Fire at London Zoo kills aardvark, meerkats believed dead", "Three-car crash in New Hampshire on Frederick E. Everett Turnpike kills one", and "Wikinews interviews Ritchie Lai of NBA Asia about the gaming industry".

annotation.notes: Unordered enumeration; singular/plural handled with |OR| because word-boundary matching makes 'meerkat' miss 'meerkats'. 'aardvark' and 'meerkats' appear in the article titles quoted in the intent, so the real discriminator is 'dog' (from the crash article) -- every negative example omits it. forbidden is left empty on purpose: a correct answer commonly contrasts ('the NBA interview mentions no animals such as cats or dogs'), so excluding candidate distractor animals would risk false rejects (guidelines trap 2). Medium confidence: an answer that lists the three plus a hallucinated extra animal would still pass -- the inherent leniency of list_match.

intent: Tell me the names of the articles where NASA scientists found some form of life in one of Neptune's satellites.

must_include: no such article |OR| no such articles |OR| no such news |OR| no such report |OR| no such coverage |OR| no article |OR| no articles |OR| no relevant article |OR| no matching article |OR| no news article |OR| there is no such |OR| there are no such |OR| there is no article |OR| there are no articles |OR| there is no news |OR| there are no news |OR| does not exist |OR| doesn't exist |OR| do not exist |OR| don't exist |OR| no results |OR| could not find |OR| couldn't find |OR| cannot find |OR| can't find |OR| did not find |OR| didn't find |OR| unable to find |OR| found no |OR| find no |OR| ^none$

annotation.notes: Unanswerable task; the only correct answer is a negative-existence claim. Adversarial review: the earlier bare alternatives 'there is no', 'there are no' and 'none' false-accepted hallucinated-article answers ('there is no doubt... the article X reports it', 'none of the other moons', '...there are no others'). Tightened every negation to be anchored to article/news/exist/find, and made the terse 'None.' answer exact via ^none$ so it cannot leak into a longer wrong sentence. Dropped a bare ^no$ anchor to cut cross-task collisions with yes/no golds ('No' is a weak answer to a 'tell me the names' question anyway). Full scope on purpose: correct answers often narrate the search first and state the verdict later. Medium because it remains an enumeration of phrasings; the residual crosstalk is with other tasks whose correct answer is also a genuine non-existence claim ('There is no article on X'), which no shape-based verifier can separate.

intent: How many articles did you find about the former prime minister of Bangladesh being sentenced to death?

must_include: none |OR| zero |OR| 0 |OR| no articles |OR| no article |OR| no news articles |OR| no matching articles |OR| not find any |OR| didn't find any |OR| couldn't find any

annotation.notes: Gold 'None' is a zero count that number_match cannot parse (extract_numbers('None') is empty), so string_match with the zero/none family is used instead. first_sentence keeps a trailing justification ('...no articles were about the death sentence') from rescuing a wrong count stated up front. Digit boundary keeps '10 articles' from matching the '0' alternative. Medium because the gold is a low-discriminative single word.

intent: Does any article on Richard Dawkins appear in the search results when you search "Richard Stallman"?

annotation.notes: Plain yes/no gold ('Yes'). must_include ['yes'] on the first sentence already discriminates: every realistic wrong answer takes the 'No' branch and carries no leading 'yes'. A must_exclude ['no'] was DROPPED because it is redundant for rejecting the wrong verdict (no wrong answer says 'yes') and only introduces false rejects -- a correct verbose answer such as 'Yes, a Dawkins article appears, though there is no other match' legitimately contains 'no' in its first sentence. Asymmetric with the 'No' tasks in this batch: there 'yes' rarely appears in a genuine negative answer, so must_exclude ['yes'] is kept.

intent: When was the article about the Texas woman who murdered her entire family published?

annotation.notes: Date gold '2024-12-19 (December 19, 2024)'. Decomposed into three required tokens (month, day, year) because the containment pattern only bridges hyphens/whitespace, not the comma in 'December 19, 2024'. Two fixes over the naive ['december |OR| 12','19','2024']: (1) the month entry now also accepts the abbreviation 'dec' (word-boundary, so it never fires inside 'december'/'decade') AND requires the numeric month '12' to sit in a date context (adjacent to 19 or 2024 via - / .). This blocks the timestamp false-accept where a wrong month carried a '12' clock reading ('November 19, 2024 at 12:30 PM'), while still accepting ISO 2024-12-19, 12/19/2024, 19-12-2024 etc. (2) the day entry accepts the ordinal '19th', which plain '19' rejects on the word boundary before 'th'. Verified: all of ISO / US-slash / EU-slash / dotted / 'Dec.' / '19th' forms pass; wrong day, wrong month (incl. iso 2024-11-19), wrong year, and the 12-timestamp near-miss all fail.

intent: Did the 2024 news on Mauritanian refugees returning from Senegal come before the news of six soldiers being killed in a Senegal ambush? If one or none of the articles can be found, then simply answer no.

annotation.notes: Standard yes/no rule. First-sentence scope keeps the justification tail ('...the ambush report is not earlier') from tripping the 'no' exclusion.

intent: Did you find any news article about a robbery on the front page (if there are multiple such articles, pick the one with the biggest headline)? If so, where did the crime take place?

must_exclude: no robbery |OR| did not find |OR| didn't find |OR| no article about |OR| no such article

annotation.notes: 'Louvre' is the discriminative half of the gold; 'Paris' is not required because 'at the Louvre Museum' alone answers the location question. scope stays 'full' because the location is usually given in a second sentence after the 'Yes'. Reviewer added a second must_exclude entry: the ^no anchor only catches answers that literally open with 'No', but a wrong answer can deny the robbery without leading with 'No' ('The front page has no robbery article, though a Louvre exhibition is featured') and still contain the token 'louvre' -- so 'no robbery'/'did not find'/'no such article' are excluded too. These negations cannot appear in a correct answer (which affirms the robbery); the natural contrastive 'no other robbery article' is safe because 'other' breaks the 'no robbery' adjacency.

intent: Was there any news on English people reporting crime using Facebook?

must_include: no |OR| not |OR| none |OR| nothing |OR| n/a |OR| nor |OR| didn't |OR| couldn't |OR| wasn't |OR| isn't

annotation.notes: Canonical yes/no rule. first_sentence keeps a justification tail ('... does not name the force ...') from rescuing a 'Yes' verdict, and the |OR| list covers the negation wordings an agent uses instead of a bare 'No' ('not', 'could not find', 'no such news').

intent: Perform the following steps: Search "Pokémon", visit the first search result, search the name of the first city in the visited article, visit the thirteenth search result, and tell me the name of the first city in that visited article.

annotation.notes: Single named entity; no city name appears in the intent, so there is no distractor to exclude and plain must_include over the full answer is safe. | SPOT-CHECK: gold value "Toronto" is correct, but the accented query "Pokemon" may tokenize to nothing in the search engine, making the task hard to execute as worded. | GOLD CORRECT ('Toronto', env-verified). Remaining concern is task executability, not the gold: the search engine's tokenizer may drop the accented query 'Pokemon'. Left for human review of the task, not the answer.

intent: Does the first search result for "David Suzuki" appear among the search results for "Toronto"?

annotation.notes: Standard yes/no recipe. first_sentence scope isolates the verdict so a correct 'Yes' followed by justification containing 'no' is not rejected. Word-boundary matching means 'Toronto' does not trip must_exclude ['no'] and 'does not' does not either.

intent: What is the maximum available length for each of the following items: the Lindy DisplayPort to HDMI cable and the Kodak HDMI Mini Cable? Answer in metres.

annotation.notes: Two measurements must both be present; exact comparison, since these are catalogue lengths, not estimates. '5 m' / '5.0 metres' variants are handled by the number parser (5.0 == 5). Medium confidence: number_match cannot detect an answer that swaps the two cables' lengths ('Lindy 1.8 m, Kodak 5 m'). A name->number binding regex was rejected because the common 'respectively' phrasing ('the Lindy and Kodak cables are 5 m and 1.8 m respectively') decouples names from numbers, so any binding spec would false-reject correct answers - a worse failure than the residual swap false-accept. The swap therefore cannot be added as a negative_example.

intent: Which cable is longer: the white Type-C to HDMI Cable or the Type-C USB Charger Cable?

annotation.notes: Trap 1: both options are named in the intent, so a wrong answer still contains the gold token 'hdmi'. must_include['hdmi'] keeps the answer on-topic; the discrimination is done by two regex exclusions. Exclusion 1 fires only when the USB Charger Cable is the subject asserted to be 'longer' (any words, not just 'is/was', so 'measures 10 ft, longer' is caught). Its leading guard '(?!than|unlike|versus|compared ... usb charger)' and the inner '(?!hdmi)' block the two correct phrasings that mention the USB cable as the loser -- 'HDMI is longer than the USB Charger Cable' and 'the HDMI cable, unlike the USB Charger Cable, is the longer one' -- so they are not false-rejected. Exclusion 2 catches the 'they are the same length' wrong answer (guarded against 'not the same length'). Medium: an exotic wrong answer that asserts USB superiority without the word 'longer'/'same length' (e.g. 'the USB cable wins on length') could still slip through.

intent: What is the total cost if I buy all the 100% polyester skirts available in the shop? If there are multiple variants (sizes, colors) of the same item, include only one.

annotation.notes: Currency total. Exact comparison (no tolerance) on purpose: an abs_tolerance of 0.01 would accept an off-by-one-cent answer such as $9.98, and every genuinely correct answer reports the price verbatim. Residual leniency: an answer that double-counts variants but still shows the unit price ('two at $9.99, total $19.98') would pass; no deterministic rule separates that from a correct answer that quotes the unit price.

intent: What would be the minimum cost to buy almonds and rice crackers?

annotation.notes: Price total. Exact comparison with no tolerance: the gold is a precise cent figure the agent reads off two product pages and adds, so an off-by-a-cent answer is a real arithmetic error, not a rounding artifact. number_match ignores the '$' and any per-item prices the agent shows alongside the total, so a breakdown answer still passes.

intent: List all the different color options available for the Nautica and GRADO SR325x headphones.

reference_answers.fuzzy_match: black black, navy navy, navy red, navy yellow, white nude, white off white

annotation.notes: Six two-word colour options. Plain containment would break on 'Black/Black' or 'Navy - Red' because the matcher only bridges hyphens and whitespace, so each item is a regex leaf allowing up to three non-letter characters between the two words. Medium confidence: an answer that lists all six plus an invented seventh option would still pass.

intent: What is the total price of all the rackets and tennis balls available in the shop? If there are multiple variants of the same item, pick one only.

must_include: zero |OR| 0 |OR| none |OR| no rackets |OR| no racket |OR| no tennis balls |OR| not available |OR| unavailable |OR| out of stock |OR| nothing |OR| no products |OR| no items |OR| not in stock
reference_answers.fuzzy_match: Zero, none of the products are available in the shop

annotation.notes: Gold is a zero total plus the reason (nothing is in stock). Dropped the earlier number_match:{value:0} gate, which had TWO defects proven by attack: it FALSE-REJECTED correct word-only answers that never write a numeral ('None of the products are available', 'they are all unavailable'), and it FALSE-ACCEPTED the '0 rackets ... $19.99' near-miss (a standalone 0 as a count plus a real positive total). The replacement keeps the broad must_include 'nothing-is-available' list (high recall, accepts numeral-free answers) and adds two must_exclude regexes that fire on any *positive* currency amount -- '$19.99' style and '19.99 dollars/usd' style -- while deliberately not matching '$0'/'$0.00'/'0 dollars'. This blocks every wrong answer that reports a positive total, whether the 0 leaks in as a count or not. Residual (hence medium): a wrong answer that pairs an unavailability phrase with a *bare* positive number carrying no currency marker ('no rackets, total 45') would leak, but that phrasing is self-contradictory and unlikely; and a correct answer that quotes a live per-item price while asserting unavailability would be over-rejected.

intent: Is there any skirt that costs less than purchasing at least one pair of jeans?

annotation.notes: Standard yes/no recipe. first_sentence keeps a price-comparison justification ('... no cheaper jeans exist') out of scope; the must_exclude then catches contradictory verdicts such as 'Yes, but no skirt is cheaper than jeans'.

intent: What's the replacement guarantee or warranty period of the 20x50 binoculars?

annotation.notes: Gold 'Three years' = quantity + unit. The original spec required only the token 'year' plus a 3 anywhere, which a wrong answer like 'a 1-year guarantee; replacements ship within 3 business days' satisfies (incidental 3 next to 'year' elsewhere). Reviewer replaced the bland must_include with an anchored regex that requires the 3 (or the word 'three') to sit immediately before 'year(s)'. The (?<![0-9]) guard keeps '13 years' out (its 3 is preceded by 1); (?![a-z]) keeps the unit exact. number_match(3) is retained as a redundant guard. The '20x50' in the intent contributes a stray 20/50, which is harmless. Accepts 'three years', '3 years', '3-year', 'three-year'; rejects '3 months', 'one/two years', '13 years', and a stray 3 that is not adjacent to the unit.

intent: Is the Wii U Microphone compatible with the Wii system?

must_include: no |OR| not |OR| none |OR| never |OR| incompatible |OR| cannot |OR| isn't |OR| doesn't |OR| wasn't |OR| aren't |OR| won't |OR| can't |OR| ^.*\bwii u\b[^.;]{0,15}\bonly\b.*$ |OR| ^.*\bonly\b[^.;]{0,20}\bwii u\b.*$

annotation.notes: Yes/no rule, first_sentence, must_exclude['yes']. The correct answer is 'No' (only Wii U compatible). Instead of a bare 'only' alternative (which would false-accept an affirmative like 'compatible with the Wii, only the older model'), the 'only' case is expressed as regexes that require 'only' next to 'Wii U' ('Wii U only' / 'only ... Wii U'), the sole phrasing under which a correct answer relies on 'only'. The contraction alternatives cover 'isn't/doesn't/won't' which contain no standalone 'not'. 'Wii' is never excluded -- a correct answer must name both systems.

intent: How many mattresses are available in the shop? (Include similar products like mattress sofas and toppers, but not related products like bed frames.)

annotation.notes: Plain count; exact match, no tolerance. number_match also accepts the spelled-out 'twelve'.

intent: How many sound bars are available under 150 USD?

annotation.notes: Count gold 'Two'; number_match handles the word, the digit and the co-occurring price threshold ('under $150') without confusion. Exact comparison. Medium because a bare '2' could appear incidentally in a wrong answer that also lists prices.

intent: How many telescopes are available for purchase?

annotation.notes: Count question with a spelled-out gold ('One'); number_match handles 'one', '1' and 'a single' is covered by the accompanying digit in practice. Gold is a bare 'One', so no extra keyword ('telescope') can be required without failing the gold check. Medium confidence for the same low-discriminative-value reason as task 39.

intent: How many Crumbl Cookies are available in the shop?

must_include: zero |OR| 0 |OR| none |OR| no crumbl |OR| no results |OR| no products |OR| no items |OR| no listings |OR| no matching |OR| no such |OR| not available |OR| not carry |OR| not sell |OR| not stock |OR| not offer |OR| not list |OR| not have any |OR| does not have |OR| not find |OR| couldn't find |OR| unable to find |OR| aren't any |OR| isn't any

annotation.notes: Gold 'Zero' cannot use number_match: the most natural correct answers ('There are no Crumbl Cookies in the shop') contain no parseable number at all and NumberMatchEvaluator returns 0.0 when it finds none. So the include list enumerates zero-quantity phrasings, and the regex exclude kills any answer that states a positive quantity of Crumbl items -- numeric or spelled ('3 Crumbl Cookies', 'one Crumbl Cookie') and vague ('a few Crumbl cookies', 'several Crumbl'), which is what a wrong answer looks like even when it also carries an incidental negation. Medium because a wrong answer with an unrelated negation and no quantity token ('...but does not carry the mini size') could still slip through the include list.

intent: How many leggings products appear when you search for the word "leggings"?

annotation.notes: Plain count; number_match parses both 'Three' and '3'. Exact comparison, no tolerance. Full scope so a preamble sentence ('I searched for leggings.') does not starve the matcher (first_sentence would false-reject a preamble-then-count answer). Medium only because an incidental integer 3 elsewhere in a wrong answer (e.g. a $3 price alongside a wrong count) would pass; that cannot be tightened without introducing false rejects, and $130.00 / $45.00 style prices do not match (word-boundary/decimal parsing verified with the oracle).

intent: I am looking for a music player to play mini vinyl records. It must be small, portable, and in black. If you find this product, could you place the order and share the confirmation code? If there is no such product or if any of the criteria are not satisfied, then please let me know.

annotation.notes: Gold is an order confirmation code - a unique opaque token, so a bare must_include is exact and cannot be produced by an agent that did not place the order. Word-boundary matching prevents a longer alphanumeric string from matching accidentally. The conditional 'if not, let me know' branch is covered because any such answer lacks the code.

intent: Could you please order the following products and share the confirmation codes with me: Hauklie Men's Polo Shirt (1 grey, size X-Large, and 1 black, size Large) and a GXP Side Table?

annotation.notes: Three confirmation codes; all must be reported. Not ordered — the intent does not fix an order for the three purchases. Codes are opaque alphanumerics, so word-boundary containment is exact.

intent: Place an order for a pair of jeans that are made of at least 60% cotton. If there are multiple options, pick any. The size must be M. Once you complete the order, share the completion code.

annotation.notes: Order completion code. A code string cannot be confused with a lookalike, so must_include is exact enough. Medium because it assumes the WebShop completion code is deterministic across runs; if codes are session-dependent this task should move to a program/network check.

intent: Place an order for a blue superhero T-shirt with a Flash logo on it. The size should be M. Once you complete the order, share the completion code.

annotation.notes: Opaque completion code. Case-insensitive word-boundary containment; no other code can collide and the code does not appear in the intent.

intent: What color is most prominent on the exterior body of the navy and yellow Nautica headphones?

annotation.notes: Trap 1: both the gold ('navy') and the wrong option ('yellow') are named in the intent as part of the product name, so a wrong answer trivially contains 'navy'. Plain must_exclude ['yellow'] would reject the very common correct restatement '...of the navy and yellow Nautica headphones is navy'. The exclusion is therefore a regex that fires on a 'yellow' only when it is NOT preceded by one of the connectives that mark a non-answer mention: 'and ' (product name), 'not '/'than '/'over ' (contrastive verdict 'navy, not yellow' / 'navy rather than yellow'), or 'with ' (accent clause 'navy, with yellow on the trim'). This keeps the guideline trap-2 contrastive and accent phrasings from false-rejecting, while a wrong answer that asserts yellow as the color ('is yellow', 'mostly yellow', bare 'Yellow', 'Yellow is most prominent') still trips because that yellow is preceded by a copula/adverb/start, not by a safe connective.

intent: What is the color of the TASYL USB lightning camera adapter?

annotation.notes: Gold is a single colour and no colour is named in the intent, so must_include['white'] carries the answer. The must_exclude['black'] plus first_sentence scope handles the realistic near-miss where the agent lists both colours and picks the wrong one ('It comes in white and black; the one listed is black'), which a plain must_include would accept. first_sentence keeps a trailing justification that mentions other variants from tripping the exclusion. Medium confidence because a correct answer phrased 'white, not black' in the leading sentence would be rejected -- an unlikely but possible phrasing for a one-word colour question.

intent: Search for the word "camera." Among the search results, which of the following colors is most common in the product pictures: white, blue, black, red, cyan, or green?

annotation.notes: Trap-1: every option is named in the intent, so a wrong answer ('white, then black') would contain the gold token. Verdict sentence must name black and none of the competing colours. Medium: a correct answer that re-lists all six options in its first sentence would be rejected.

intent: Is there a remote in the product picture of the 4-Channel Wireless Bluetooth Power Amplifier?

annotation.notes: Yes/no recipe with first_sentence scope so a correct 'Yes' followed by 'the remote is small and there is no other accessory' is still accepted. 'not' and 'none' do not match must_exclude ['no'] under word-boundary matching.

intent: Which of the following items are available in the shop: Ice-cream, Dog food, Mushroom, Superglue?

annotation.notes: Trap 1: all four candidate items are named in the intent, so a wrong answer ('Ice-cream and Mushroom are available') would satisfy a plain must_include. Standard recipe: first_sentence scope, require the correct item, exclude the three distractors from the verdict sentence. A correct answer is free to list the unavailable items after the verdict sentence. Medium because a correct answer that crams the negatives into the same sentence with a semicolon ('Mushroom is available; Ice-cream, Dog food and Superglue are not') would be rejected.

intent: I am looking for a tooth powder that contains fluoride, as I heard it is good for dental health. It would be great if the product is also herbal and vegan. Please tell me the product name of the best match you find.

reference_answers.fuzzy_match: 2 Pcs Eva Smokers with Fluorine Natural Herbal Halal Islamic Toothpowder Powder 40gm

annotation.notes: Product-name answer. The only token combination unique to the gold product is 'Eva Smokers' — the rest of the title ('Fluorine', 'Herbal', 'Toothpowder', '40gm') is generic for this category and would let a different tooth-powder product pass. The singular alternative covers 'Eva Smoker's'. Requiring only the distinctive brand fragment lets an agent shorten or reorder the very long title.

intent: Does the Salt & Sugar Bundle Kit reduce the appearance of acne scars?

must_include: yes |OR| does reduce |OR| reduces |OR| helps reduce |OR| can reduce

annotation.notes: Yes/no gold. first_sentence isolates the verdict from any justification. 'reduces' is offered as an alternative because a correct answer may assert the claim without the literal word 'yes'; the negated form 'does not reduce' cannot match either alternative ('reduce' != 'reduces' under word-boundary matching, and 'does reduce' is not contained in 'does not reduce'). 'not' is deliberately NOT excluded (trap 2) so hedged-but-correct answers survive.

intent: How many times does the phrase "baking soda" appear on the Arm & Hammer Toothpaste product page (including Description, Features, Reviews)?

annotation.notes: A count ('Eight times'). number_match parses both the word 'eight' and the digit 8. A verbose answer that also breaks the count down by section still contains 8.

intent: Is there any pink USB-C charging cable available in the shop? If so, please place the order for one and share the confirmation code with me.

must_include: ^no(?![a-z0-9]).*$ |OR| ^none(?![a-z0-9]).*$ |OR| no pink |OR| no usb |OR| no cable |OR| no charging |OR| no such |OR| no matching |OR| no results |OR| none available |OR| not available |OR| not carry |OR| not sell |OR| not stock |OR| not offer |OR| not have |OR| not find |OR| couldn't find |OR| could not find |OR| unable to find |OR| isn't any |OR| aren't any |OR| not any
reference_answers.fuzzy_match: No pink USB-C charging cable is available

annotation.notes: Effectively a yes/no gold with a conditional follow-up: since no pink cable exists there is no confirmation code to report, so the only correct answer is a negative verdict. Scoped to the first sentence and must_exclude 'yes' so that 'Yes, I ordered one...' fails even when the tail mentions unavailability. The include list is a regex requiring the verdict sentence to *open* with 'no'/'none', plus negation phrases bound to a verb or to the product; that keeps it from firing on an incidental 'no' buried inside an affirmative answer.

intent: Find the most recent sports event mentioned in Brazil's Wikipedia article. Can you find a news article about that event? If so, please tell me the title of the news article.

must_include: rio de janeiro to host 2016 olympics |OR| rio de janeiro to host the 2016 olympics |OR| rio to host 2016 olympics
reference_answers.fuzzy_match: Rio de Janeiro to host 2016 Olympics

annotation.notes: The task asks for a news article title, so the whole distinctive title phrase is required rather than its component tokens. Requiring only 'rio de janeiro' + '2016' + 'olympics' would accept the common wrong answer that identifies the event but reports that no news article exists.

intent: I need you to cross-reference something. Go to the Paris Agreement article on Wiki and find the last article in the 'Related Pages' or 'See also' section. Search the title of that article on News, visit the top result, and check if the news article contains the word 'Russia'.

annotation.notes: Standard yes/no recipe. The verdict comes first and the cross-reference trail ('the last See also entry was ...') stays outside the first_sentence scope, so 'no' can be excluded safely.

intent: Find the country of origin of the rice used in the Crunchmaster Rice Crackers. Visit the Wikipedia article on that country and tell me the last word of the first paragraph.

annotation.notes: Trap 3: 'people' is a low-discriminative token that can appear incidentally in a two-hop answer that also names the country. Scoping to the first sentence would be stricter but rejects the very common correct shape 'The rice comes from Thailand. The last word of the first paragraph is people.', so full scope is used. Negatives probe wrong last-words including one that gets the intermediate country right.

intent: Verify if the BioCorneum Advanced Scar Treatment Gel from Shop is FDA-cleared. If so, then search "Food and Drug Administration" on Wiki and tell me when the agency was formed. Otherwise, search "Food & Drug Administration" on News and tell me the title of the first search result.

annotation.notes: Conditional task whose correct branch ends in a year. A year is literal digits with no magnitude ambiguity, so string_match is preferred over number_match. Full scope is required: correct answers commonly open with the FDA-cleared verdict and give the year in a later sentence. intent: Visit the Wiki article on "Espadrille" and find the first country mentioned in that article. Which of the following sites: Wiki, News, or Shop, have an article about that country or a product from that country?
additional_instructions:

First exclusion is a negation-aware regex: it fires only when 'shop' appears and the answer contains no negation token anywhere, which kills 'Wiki, News, and Shop' / 'all three sites ... Wiki, News and Shop' while leaving every 'but not Shop' / 'the Shop does not' phrasing intact. Second exclusion catches the mirror-image wrong answer that names News only to deny it ('Only Wiki; News and Shop have nothing'), which the first exclusion would let through because it contains a negation. Medium confidence: a wrong 'all three' answer that happens to contain an unrelated 'not' would still be accepted.

intent: Verify whether Sony's net profit fell significantly in 2024 or 2025. If so, visit the Sony's Wiki article and identify the first product mentioned on that page. Can you find that exact product in the Shop? If so, place the order and share the confirmation code with me. If any of the above conditions cannot be satisfied, state that explicitly.
additional_instructions:
Perform these instructions to complete the task:

1. Go to News and search "Sony's net profit fell significantly".
2. You will find an article "Sony net profit falls by 95%". Click on the article and you will see that the publication date is from 2024. Hence it is a valid article. Remember this fact.

must_include: ^.*\b(?:not available|unavailable|not in the shop|not sold|not listed|not carried|no playstation|no such product|no results|not find|not found|does not sell|doesn't sell|does not carry|doesn't carry|does not have|doesn't have|does not stock|doesn't stock)\b.*$

annotation.notes: Multi-site conditional task whose gold is the explicit 'condition not satisfiable' statement. The first must_include entry is a regex over the unavailability phrasings an agent uses ('not available', 'could not find', 'the shop does not sell it', 'no PlayStation'). The second entry (playstation|product|shop|store|console) ties that unavailability claim to the product/shop, so an abandonment for the WRONG reason that happens to use an unavailability word - e.g. 'I could not find the article about Sony's profit' - no longer false-accepts. Wrong answers with a fabricated confirmation code contain no unavailability word. Medium because the spec verifies the unavailable-in-shop verdict, not the full chain of reasoning (profit fell, PlayStation is the first product).

intent: I love the Matrix movie series. Please find related Wiki articles, news, and products from the Shop. If there are multiple entries on each site, pick the one you think is the most relevant. must_include: no relevant news |OR| no news |OR| no relevant article |OR| no article |OR| none found
no relevant product |OR| no product |OR| no matching product |OR| no products
reference_answers.fuzzy_match:
Wiki: The Matrix
News: No relevant news found.
Shop: No relevant product found.

Tightened: the earlier spec shared the generic alternatives 'none'/'not found'/'no result'/'no relevant' between the news and product requirements, so a single incidental 'none' (e.g. 'none of the shop items matched, but The Matrix Blu-ray is closest') satisfied both while the answer actually surfaced a real news item and product — a verified false accept. News-absence and product-absence now use disjoint, site-qualified phrases. Both 'non-typical' AND 'long sleeve' are required (not an OR): Legendary Whitetails ships several 'Non-Typical' line items and several 'Long Sleeve' items, so an OR would false-accept a *different* Legendary Whitetails product (e.g. a 'Non-Typical Hoodie' or a 'Camo Long Sleeve Tee') -- verified against the oracle. intent: Search "Ruffles Ridged Potato Chips" on Shop and find the country of origin. Search for the name of that country on News and visit the second news article in the search results. What is the last word in the visited article?

2. Open the product page and each tab individually. Click on the features tab, identify the country of origin listed, which is the United States. Remember this fact.

Word-boundary matching means 'outrage' does not fire on 'outrageous' or 'outraged', which is the near-miss to guard for a 'last word' task. scope stays 'full' (NOT first_sentence): the two-part task means a correct answer legitimately lands in a later sentence, e.g. 'The country of origin is the United States. The last word is Outrage.' Medium confidence: the gold word is also the article's likely topic, so a wrong last-word answer that discusses the same story ('the last word is protests, reflecting the public outrage') could mention 'outrage' incidentally and be falsely accepted -- there is no deterministic anchor that separates 'outrage as the last word' from 'outrage as the subject'.

intent: Search "chips" on News. If the first article is about snack chips, then go to Shop, search "chips", and place an order for the first chips product you find in the search results. Otherwise, let me know that the first article is not about snack chips.
additional_instructions:
Perform these instructions to complete the task:

1. On News, search for "chips" and open the first article in the results.
2. Determine whether the article is about snack chips (potato chips, corn chips, etc.), not electronic chips or other meanings.
3. If the article IS about snack chips:

The regex requires a negation word within 40 characters (and inside the same sentence) of 'snack', which distinguishes 'not about snack chips' from 'about snack chips, not microchips'. The must_exclude regex matches a 10-character mixed letter/digit token, i.e. a webshop confirmation code — a correct answer places no order and so can never contain one, while the wrong branch always reports one. Medium confidence because the negation is matched by pattern rather than by a fixed token.

intent: What happened at the end of the book "The Neptune Secret"?

must_include: no such book |OR| no such title |OR| no such novel |OR| no such publication |OR| no book called |OR| no book titled |OR| no book named |OR| no book by that |OR| no book with that |OR| does not exist |OR| doesn't exist |OR| do not exist |OR| don't exist |OR| not exist |OR| no matching book |OR| not a real book |OR| not a real novel |OR| not a book |OR| find any book |OR| find any such book |OR| find no book |OR| found no book |OR| not appear to exist |OR| not seem to exist |OR| nonexistent |OR| non existent |OR| isn't a real book |OR| is not a real book

Replaced 'no book' with the specific nonexistence forms ('no book called/titled/named/by that title') and added 'find any book' so 'I couldn't find any book by that title' is still accepted.
